chapter 01 Self-attention The transformer

chapter 01 · transformer — part 1 of 2

Self-attention

The one idea the transformer is built around: every position emits a query, every position advertises a key, and the match between them decides who reads from whom. Derived here from the problem it solves, then compared against the architectures it replaced.

In one sentence. Self-attention lets every position pull in information from the other positions it judges relevant — with “relevant” being learned, directional, and recomputed for every input.

Three near-misses are worth naming, because each one is a real idea that attention deliberately is not:

not quite…why not
“it finds correlations in the sequence”Correlation is symmetric and fixed. Attention is asymmetric on purpose — a pronoun seeks its antecedent, not the reverse — and its notion of relatedness is learned, not a statistic.
“it finds the similar tokens”Relevant is usually not similar. A verb wants a noun; a closing bracket wants its opener. See the four reasons below.
“it finds relationships”Finding is only half. The scores are not the output — they are routing weights that decide which values get mixed into each position. Attention moves information; it does not report an analysis.

If that is all you take from this page, it is the right half. Everything below is why each of those words — learned, directional, recomputed — is load-bearing.

Where this sits in the model

Before the mechanism, the map — because attention on its own predicts nothing. It is one sub-layer, inside a block, that repeats:

Three things follow, and they are what makes the rest of the page make sense:

  • Attention's output is not a prediction. It is an edit added to a running vector. The prediction happens once, at the very end, from the last position's final vector.
  • Shape in = shape out. n × d_model both ways. Attention mixes across positions without changing the container — which is precisely why you can run 100 of them in a row.
  • Each block does one of each. Attention is the only step where a token can see another token; the MLP then processes every position alone. Mix, think, mix, think, N times.

So when the rest of this page says "the output b¹", that vector is not an answer — it is what gets added to position 1's running total before the next block sees it. The full path, tokenizer to sampled token, is part 2.

The problem attention is solving

Before the mechanism, the goal. Given a sequence of vectors a¹…aⁿ, each output bi must be built from whichever other positions actually matter for position i — and which ones matter differs for every token, every sentence, and every layer. It can't be fixed in advance, so it has to be computed from the content itself:

Why relevance has to be learned

The obvious shortcut is to score that arrow with the raw dot product aⁱ · aʲ. It fails four times over, each one fatal on its own:

Raw aⁱ · aʲ is…so…
symmetrica pronoun could never attend to its antecedent more than the reverse — but relevance is directional
diagonal-dominated
aⁱ·aⁱ = |aⁱ|² is the largest entry in its row		every token attends almost entirely to itself; the layer collapses to the identity map
the same everywhere
there is only one identity matrix		every head and every layer computes the same pattern — multi-head specialization becomes impossible
measuring the wrong thing“relevant” usually isn't “similar”: a closing bracket wants its opener, not another bracket

The fix is to stop comparing the token vectors directly. Project each token's own vector aⁱ through two learned matrices first, then compare the results — and all four problems go at once. Here is why that works, and why it is less of a leap than it looks.

“Project” just means multiply by a matrix. qⁱ = Wqaⁱ takes the token's full representation and re-expresses it in a smaller space. Nothing is added; a particular view is extracted from what was already there. The shapes, with typical numbers:

aⁱ   d_model × 1      4096 × 1     the token, as it arrives
Wq   d_k × d_model    128 × 4096   learned, shared by every position
qⁱ   d_k × 1          128 × 1     = Wqaⁱ   (128×4096)(4096×1)

Wk has the same shape as Wq, so queries and keys land in the same 128-dimensional space and can be compared. Wv is d_v × d_model, and d_v need not equal d_k — the payload is not compared against anything, so it is free to be a different size.

The notebook writes these transposed, and it is the same thing. This page follows the slides: tokens are columns, so Wq is d_k × d_model and q = Wqa. PyTorch — and practice/p0_attention — stack tokens as rows, so the matrix is d_model × d_k and you write Q = X @ W_q. Transpose one convention and you get the other. Check which a source uses before matching shapes.

The same vector aⁱ goes through both matrices, giving two different views of the one token:

  • qⁱ = Wqaⁱ — what this token is looking for
  • kⁱ = Wkaⁱ — what this token offers to be found by

Every token produces both, because every token both asks and answers. The score that matters is one token's query against another's key — never query against query. (A pedantic note, since you may know the term: in linear algebra a projection is idempotent, P² = P. These are not. ML uses “project” loosely for any linear map into another space.)

The dot product already has a hidden assumption

Write the raw dot product as a matrix sandwich and the assumption becomes visible:

aⁱ · aʲ  =  aⁱᵀ I aʲ        # the identity matrix was there all along

So scoring with a bare dot product is not the assumption-free choice. It is the choice M = I: every dimension matters equally, and a feature may only ever match itself. Dimension 7 of one token can only be compared against dimension 7 of another. Every one of the four failures above is that one constraint, seen from a different side.

The generalisation writes itself. Replace I with something learned:

score(aⁱ, aʲ)  =  aⁱᵀ M aʲ      # M learned instead of assumed

What the off-diagonal entries buy, and it is the whole point. M[7,3] ≠ 0 means dimension 7 of the query token is compared against dimension 3 of the key token. Relevance stops meaning "these two are alike" and starts meaning a learned correspondence between two different features.

That is what lets a verb find its subject. The verb does not look for a token resembling a verb; it looks for "is a noun, nominative, singular" — a different feature from the one it carries. With M = I that question cannot even be posed.

Why factor M, instead of just learning it

Now substitute the projections and the factorisation falls out in one line:

qⁱ = Wqaⁱ ,  kʲ = Wkaʲ

qⁱ · kʲ  =  (Wqaⁱ)ᵀ (Wkaʲ)  =  aⁱᵀ (Wq)ᵀWk aʲ  =  aⁱᵀ M aʲ

Query-and-key is not a different idea from the bilinear form — it is the bilinear form, written as two factors. Three things make the factored version the one you want:

learn M directlylearn Wq, Wk
parameters d_model 4096, d_k 1284096² ≈ 16.8 M per head2 × 4096×128 ≈ 1.0 M — 16× fewer
rankfull — free to use all 4096 directionsat most d_k = 128. A built-in regulariser: the head must commit to a small subspace
cost of n² scoresaⁱᵀMaʲ per pair, or re-factor it anywayproject once, then one matmul QKᵀ for every pair at once

The last row is the practical one. q and k are reusable intermediates: compute each token's query and key once, and every pairwise score is a single matrix multiply. Keep M whole and you would factor it yourself to get that.

How anyone came up with it

It was not invented from nothing — it arrived by two small steps, each fixing the step before:

  1. Additive attention (Bahdanau, 2014) scored a query–key pair by running both through a small network: score = vᵀ tanh(W₁h + W₂s). Learned and expressive, but it is an MLP (multi-layer perceptron) per pair — there is no way to batch n² of them into a matmul.
  2. Multiplicative attention (Luong, 2015) replaced that network with hᵀWs — the bilinear form, four years before the transformer. Same expressiveness for the job, one matmul instead of an MLP.
  3. The transformer factored that W into Wq and Wk, which bought the parameter and rank savings above, ran several in parallel as heads, and pointed it at a sequence's own tokens instead of at a separate encoder.

If you have done metric learning, you have already done this. The Mahalanobis distance (a−b)ᵀM(a−b) is exactly the same move: Euclidean distance is the M = I special case, and learning M lets the data say which directions matter and which features correspond. Attention's score is the bilinear cousin, learned end to end for one question — which token should I read next? — and factored so that all n² answers come out of one matrix multiply.

The mechanism: score, weight, read

So the arrow gets answered like this:

Two details the picture leaves out, both load-bearing:

  • The projections narrow. Wq, Wk map d_model (≈4096) down to d_k (≈128), so each head compares only the slice it cares about — and scoring all pairs gets ~32× cheaper.
  • The score is scaled: α = q·k/√d_k. The variance of a dot product grows with d_k, and unscaled scores of ±11 saturate the softmax into a near one-hot distribution where the gradient vanishes.

Weights: softmax over the scores

Now run that module once per position and normalize the results — one query against every key:

Reading that slide: the black dot is a dot product, and α comes in two flavours.

  • α1,i — the raw score, before softmax. Each black dot computes one.
  • α′1,i — the same thing after softmax (note the prime). These are the weights that sum to 1.

The subscripts are αquery,key: the first index is who is asking, the second is who is being looked at. So α1,3 is "how much does position 1 want position 3", which is not the same as α3,1.

So α1,1 is position 1 scoring itself — one dot product between two vectors of length d_k:

q¹ = Wqa¹        k¹ = Wka¹        # same a¹, different matrices

α₁,₁ = q¹ · k¹ = Σd q¹d k¹d = q¹₁k¹₁ + q¹₂k¹₂ + … + q¹128k¹128

# one number. Real implementations divide it by √d_k.

And here is the payoff from earlier. q¹ and k¹ are built from the same a¹ but through different matrices, so they are different vectors — and α1,1 has no reason to be the largest score in its row. Score the raw vectors instead and the self-score would be a¹·a¹ = |a¹|², necessarily the biggest entry, and every token would attend to itself. The diagonal stops dominating precisely because Wq ≠ Wk.

Softmax is doing three separate jobs here:

  • Normalizes — weights sum to 1, so the output is a weighted average of values, bounded however long the sequence gets.
  • Sharpens — exponentiating turns a modest score gap into a large weight gap, approximating a hard lookup while staying differentiable.
  • Never assigns exactly zero — every position keeps some gradient, so one the model currently ignores can still learn to become relevant. A hard argmax would give the lookup and kill the gradient.

The payload: a third projection

Those weights are still only an addressing scheme — they say where to read, not what is read. A third projection supplies the payload:

Why three projections, and how they relate

The reason is not that three is a nice number. Each token plays three different roles in a single attention step, and the roles need different information out of the same vector.

Take the token sat in “The cat sat down”. Within one layer it is used three separate times, with three different partners:

rolewhenwhat it needs to sayvector
the askercomputing sat's own output“I am a verb — I need my subject”q = Wqa
a candidateevery other token is deciding what to read“I am a past-tense verb” — so others can judge whether to pick mek = Wka
a sourceonce something has picked itthe actual content to hand overv = Wva

It is a dictionary where every token is simultaneously a lookup and an entry. In ordinary Python d["apple"] → "a red fruit": the key is what you match against, the value is what you get back, and the query is what the caller brings. An entry needs two things; a lookup needs a third. Attention asks every token to be both at once — so it needs all three.

Now collapse them and watch each failure:

if you tie…what breaks
query = key“what I am looking for” becomes “what I advertise”. A verb hunting for a noun would advertise itself as hunting for a noun — so other verbs hunting for nouns would match it. The question silently turns from who answers me? into who is like me?, which is the symmetric failure from the table above.
key = value“how I am found” becomes “what I give”. Look a token up by its grammatical role and you receive… its grammatical role. You want to find something by one property and be handed a different one — that is the whole point of a lookup.
all threeattention degenerates into a similarity filter over the raw embeddings: everything attends to whatever resembles it, and nothing is learned.

So: K answers “should you read me?” and V answers “here is what you get.” Keeping them apart lets a token be indexed by one property and contribute another — findable by its grammatical role while handing over its meaning. That decoupling of address from payload is what makes attention a memory rather than a similarity filter.

…and how they relate

They are not three independent knobs. They pair up — and the pairs, not the matrices, are what the model actually learns.

Wq and Wk never appear on their own. They only ever reach the loss through their product:

score  =  aⁱᵀ (Wq)ᵀWk aʲ        # only the product is identified

Which means the split between them is arbitrary. Rotate the query space by any rotation R and the key space by the same R, and every score is unchanged — the rotations cancel inside the dot product. There are infinitely many (Wq, Wk) pairs giving an identical model.

So do not try to interpret a single dimension of q or k. It has no meaning on its own — only the angles between queries and keys do. Two training runs will produce completely different Wq matrices and the same attention patterns.

Wv is in a different business entirely, and it pairs with a fourth matrix: Wo, the projection that merges the heads back together at the end of the layer. So the four matrices make two circuits, each answering one question:

circuitproductdecides
QK(Wq)ᵀWkwhere to read from — it only ever produces attention weights, and never touches the content that gets moved
OVWoWvwhat gets written once a position has been selected — it never influences where the attention goes

That separation is why the ds differ. Wq and Wk must share an output width d_k, or their dot product would not typecheck. Wv is under no such constraint — d_v only has to match what Wo expects, because a value is never compared with anything, only summed.

It is also the cleanest way to read a trained head: the QK circuit is the head's question, the OV circuit is its answer. p1 in practice/ separates exactly these — a previous-token head and an induction head differ entirely in their QK circuits.

Every position takes the same route

Everything drawn so far computes b¹ only. Position 2 uses its own query against the same four keys and the same weights — a different row:

And because no output reads another output, all of them can be computed at once:

The batched form: four matmuls and a softmax

That independence is what licenses it — and it is where the whole operation collapses to one line. Three steps get you there. First the projections: because every position runs the same Wq against its own input, computing qi = Wqai position by position is the same arithmetic as one matmul against the whole sequence:

Second, the scores. One query against all keys was a row; all queries against all keys is the whole matrix:

Third and last, the read-out. The weighted sum that produced b¹ is itself a matmul once the weights sit in a matrix:

Put the three together and you get the line every implementation writes:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( QKᵀ / √d_k ) V

#  QKᵀ        all n² scores in one matmul       → [n, n]
#  / √d_k     keeps softmax out of saturation
#  softmax    each row becomes a distribution over positions
#  @ V        each output = weighted average of values → [n, d_v]

And the entire layer, on one slide:

Don't let the transposes confuse you — they're the same equation. The slides write A = KᵀQ and O = V A′; the paper and every framework write softmax(QKᵀ)V. The difference is purely bookkeeping: the slides stack each vector as a column of the matrix, while PyTorch stacks each token as a row (shape [batch, seq, dim], because that's how sequences arrive). Transpose one convention and you get the other — Oᵀ = A′ᵀVᵀ. Worth noticing which convention a source uses before trying to match its shapes, since it also flips whether softmax runs over rows or columns.

Parallel to train, sequential to generate

The catch is that parallelism is a training property. At inference an LLM still emits one token at a time, each conditioned on the last — so generation is sequential even though the forward pass is not. That asymmetry is why training scales with hardware and decoding does not, and it is the root of the KV-cache and every batching trick in serving.

Multi-head: several kinds of relevance at once

Everything so far builds one notion of relevance — one M = (Wq)ᵀWk, one attention pattern. But a token usually needs several relations at the same time: its syntactic head, the last mention of its referent, the topic of the paragraph.

Why one head cannot just do all three — the softmax is the bottleneck. Its weights sum to 1, so a head has a fixed budget of attention to spend. Needing both the subject and the antecedent, one head can only split it:

one head    α′ = [ .5 subject , .5 antecedent ]
            b  = 0.5·vsubject + 0.5·vantecedent     # one blended vector

two heads   head 1  α′ = [ 1.0 subject    ] → b¹ = vsubject
            head 2  α′ = [ 1.0 antecedent ] → b² = vantecedent   # kept apart

The damage is not just the halved weights — it is that b is a blend nothing downstream can un-mix. Two heads each spend a full budget, and their results land in different slices of the output, so WO can route them separately. Multi-head is not extra capacity so much as several independent budgets with separable outputs.

So run several in parallel instead:

Which leaves one problem: there are now several partial outputs where the layer must emit a single vector. Concatenate and project:

Heads split the width, they don't add to it. The intuitive worry is that 32 heads cost 32× — they don't. With d_model = 4096 and 32 heads, each head works in d_k = 128, and 32 × 128 = 4096: the same total dimension, partitioned rather than duplicated. Parameters and FLOPs are essentially unchanged from one wide head. What you get for free is independence — 32 separate score matrices that can specialize, instead of one that must compromise. That is close to the best trade in the architecture, and it's why every model uses many heads.

What the attention scores are

Inside the forward pass the attention matrix has exactly one job, and naming it precisely is worth more than any analogy: A holds the connection weights of the only path by which information moves between positions — and unlike every other weight in the network, they are computed from the input at run time rather than learned and frozen.

A transformer block is two alternating operations, and the division is absolute:

sub-layermoves information…its weights are…
attentionacross positions — the only place a token can see another tokencomputed per input: A = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k), fresh for every sequence, every layer, every head
feed-forwardnowhere — each position is transformed alone, in parallel, never consulting its neighbourslearned and fixed after training

So the scores are not a feature, a score in the ranking sense, or an intermediate value that gets added to anything. They are wiring. An MLP's connectivity is fixed; a CNN's is fixed and local. Attention's is recomputed for every example — which is the whole reason the same layer handles "the cat sat" and a 100 000-token document.

And they carry no content whatsoever. This is the QK/OV split from earlier, stated as a forward-pass fact: A decides where to read from and V supplies what is read. Every number in A is a non-negative weight summing to 1 along a row — it cannot encode meaning, only proportions. Swap in different values and the routing is unchanged; swap in different scores and the same values get mixed differently.

In residual-stream terms: each layer reads from the stream and writes back into it. The scores decide which positions get read; the OV circuit decides what gets written. Everything a transformer does over long range is built from that one move, stacked.

And what they are good for outside it

Being the most legible thing a transformer produces, A also gets read from the outside, four ways:

usewhat it means
diagnosticsScore a head by its pattern to find out what it does. p1 in practice/ identifies induction heads exactly this way — and pairs every score with a control, which is what makes it evidence rather than a picture.
alignmentThe original use: in translation, the attention map between source and target is a soft word alignment, read straight off the matrix.
copying / pointingUse the distribution directly as an output over input positions, to copy a token rather than generate one — pointer networks and copy mechanisms. Here the weights are not an intermediate at all; they are the answer.
efficiencyObserved sparsity motivates sparse, local and sliding-window attention, and informs what a KV cache must keep.

🔴 Attention weights are not explanations, and this is a real argument, not a caveat for politeness. Attention is not Explanation (Jain & Wallace, 2019) showed that you can often find a very different attention distribution that yields the same prediction — so the weights you observed were not the ones responsible. Attention is not not Explanation (Wiegreffe & Pinter, 2019) pushed back on how that was tested. The defensible reading: attention shows where information could have flowed, not that it did, nor that it mattered.

And do not assume every head earns its place — Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One? (Michel et al., 2019) found a large share can be pruned at test time with little loss. Specialized heads are real; every head being specialized is not.

Position: the one thing attention cannot see

Look back at the formula and try to find the index i in it. It isn't there. Scores depend on q and k, the output is a sum over all positions — nothing anywhere refers to where a token sits. Shuffle the inputs and the outputs come back shuffled the same way, otherwise unchanged. Attention is permutation-equivariant, which means "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are, to a bare attention layer, the same input. Position has to be injected by hand:

Why not just append the position as a number? It is the first thing anyone tries, and it fails three ways: the value is unbounded (position 4000 arrives as a feature 4000× larger than position 1 and swamps the layer norm), it is one dimension against thousands of content dimensions, and it does not generalise — a model trained to 2 048 has never seen the number 5 000 and has no reason to treat it sensibly. You want something bounded, high-dimensional, and smooth in position. Sinusoids are all three.

Why sinusoids, and not any other bounded code

"Continuous binary counter" explains why the pattern never repeats, but not why these functions. The real reason is one property, and it is the whole design:

PE(pos)2i   = sin(ωi · pos)        ωi = 1 / 100002i/d
PE(pos)2i+1 = cos(ωi · pos)

# take any fixed offset k. For each (sin, cos) pair:

[ sin(ω(pos+k)) ]   [ cos ωk   sin ωk ] [ sin(ω·pos) ]
[ cos(ω(pos+k)) ] = [ -sin ωk  cos ωk ] [ cos(ω·pos) ]
                     └──── R(ωk) ────┘   # a rotation. Depends on k, NOT on pos.

PE(pos+k) is a fixed linear function of PE(pos). Each (sin, cos) pair is a 2D vector spinning at its own rate, and moving k steps rotates every pair by an angle that depends only on k. So a single learned linear map — which is exactly what Wq and Wk are — can implement "attend three tokens back", and the same map works at position 5 and position 500.

Which makes RoPE a small step, not a new idea. Sinusoidal encoding gives you rotation-by-position, then adds it to the input and hopes the projections recover it. RoPE applies the same rotation directly to q and k. Then in the score the two rotations meet:

(Rmq) · (Rnk)  =  q ᵀRmᵀRn k  =  q ᵀRn−m k      # absolute positions cancel

The score depends only on n − m, the relative offset. Nothing is added to the residual stream, nothing has to be recovered, and a distance of 3 means the same thing at position 10 and position 10 000 — which is why it extrapolates past the training length so much better.

Two things about that slide have dated, and both are worth knowing. "Hand-crafted" is no longer the norm — GPT-2 and BERT learned absolute position embeddings instead, and current models overwhelmingly use RoPE, which doesn't add anything to ai at all. RoPE rotates q and k by an angle proportional to position, so the dot product between them ends up depending only on their relative distance — which is usually what actually matters, and extrapolates to lengths never seen in training far better than absolute encodings do.

And the choice to add rather than concatenate looks lossy at first — you're summing position into the same coordinates that carry meaning. It works because d_model is large: in a few thousand dimensions there is ample room for position and content to occupy near-orthogonal subspaces, and the projections can read either one back out. Concatenating would have cost extra width for the same effect.

The same layer, other modalities

Nothing in the derivation assumed language. Attention needs only a set of vectors — so anything you can express that way is fair game:

That reframing was enough to rebuild much of computer vision around attention:

Spot the disguise in the SAGAN diagram. Those three 1×1 convolutions producing f(x), g(x), h(x) are Wq, Wk, Wv — a 1×1 convolution is precisely a per-position linear projection, applied identically at every location. Follow the arrows: f and g multiply and softmax into an attention map, which then weights h. It is the equation you already know, drawn in the vocabulary of convnets.

Speech fits the same mould, but it's where the O(n²) bill comes due:

That slide is more current than it looks. Truncated attention is the ancestor of every long-context method in production today — sliding-window attention, Longformer's local-plus-global pattern, and the sparse and linear attention families all make the same bet, that most of the L × L matrix isn't worth computing. (FlashAttention is the exception that proves the rule: it keeps every entry and instead avoids ever writing the matrix to memory.) This is the same O(n²) wall flagged back at the attention matrix, and in §3 it reappears as the constraint that governs how much an agent can hold in context.

Self-attention vs CNN: the same operation, one with its receptive field frozen

Once an image is a vector set, the obvious question is what separates attention from the convolution that ruled vision for a decade. The answer is sharper than "they're different architectures":

That isn't just an analogy — it holds formally:

Being the more flexible model is not automatically an advantage, and the data settles it:

This chart is the whole architecture story of the last decade, in one picture. A CNN's hard-coded locality is a prior — free knowledge, handed over before training starts, that nearby pixels belong together. When data is scarce that prior is worth more than anything the model could induce, so the CNN wins. When data is abundant the same prior becomes a ceiling: the model is forbidden from learning a better rule than the one you imposed. Attention has less built in and therefore needs more data — and given that data, it learns a rule your kernel size could never encode.

The identical trade played out in language: LSTMs carried a strong sequential prior and beat early transformers on small corpora, then lost decisively once corpora reached internet scale. It's the reason §2's story is about scale rather than about cleverer architectures — the flexible model plus more data beats the constrained model, as soon as you can afford the data.

Self-attention vs RNN: why the recurrence went away

Before attention, sequences meant recurrence: carry a memory vector forward, one step at a time. The slide puts the two side by side, and the two red annotations are the entire argument:

Notice that attention is not the cheaper option. An RNN layer costs O(n) with a fixed-size state; attention costs O(n²) and stores the whole matrix. What attention did was convert a latency problem into a throughput problem — and throughput is something you can buy more GPUs for, while a sequential dependency is something no amount of hardware can remove. That trade is the entire reason the architecture won.

The paper cited on that slide closes the loop. "Transformers are RNNs" (arXiv:2006.16236) shows that with linear attention, an autoregressive transformer is expressible as an RNN with constant-size state. And this isn't only a theoretical curiosity — recall from earlier that generation is sequential anyway: a decoding transformer with a KV cache is already a recurrent model whose state happens to grow. The RNN never really lost at inference. It lost at training, which is where the parallelism was worth having.

Graphs: attention with the edges supplied

One last case, and it retro-fits everything above into a single idea. A graph is already a set of vectors — one per node — so attention applies directly. But a graph also tells you something extra: which pairs are actually related.

The unifying idea: structure enters through the mask. Every variant in this whole section is the same layer with a different rule about which cells of the score matrix are allowed to be non-zero.

  • No mask → every position sees every other. Plain self-attention, an encoder, BERT.
  • Causal mask → position i sees only ≤ i. Language modelling, every decoder, step 4 below.
  • Window mask → each position sees a local range. Truncated attention for speech, and every sliding-window long-context scheme.
  • Adjacency mask → only connected nodes. Graph attention networks.
  • Fixed offset per head → the convolution, as the Cordonnier construction showed.

So the honest one-line summary of the last several subsections: attention is a general mechanism for routing information between positions, and each architecture is a prior about which routes are worth allowing. Choose the mask and you've chosen the architecture.

Go and run one. Attention is the rare idea where the interactive explanations are genuinely better than the prose — including this page's. Seven, ordered by how much work they ask of you. The first two are hands-on labs in this repo; the third is the source of this page's own figures. All verified live 2026-10-09.

p0 · attention by hand
in this repo · open the notebook in Colab		 See it, then build it. A notebook steps through one attention layer with numbers small enough to check by hand — change a value, re-run, watch the pattern move. Then attention_lab.py makes you implement single-head, multi-head and masked attention yourself, checked against your own longhand loop. The mechanism, in your hands. Written for exactly this point — you have watched the lectures and want to do it. It makes you prove the two things slides cannot: that heads never mix (perturb one head's keys, the others must come out bit-identical) and that masking makes the past independent of the future (rewrite later tokens, earlier outputs must not move). It also measures why 1/√d_k exists instead of asserting it.
p1 · heads learn an algorithm
in this repo · practice/p1_induction_heads/ · GPU, ~19 s		 Train a 41k-parameter transformer until it discovers a circuit, then score every head: content-matching vs positional reflex. What multi-head is FOR. p0 proves heads cannot mix; this shows why that matters — the model splits one algorithm across two layers, a previous-token head in layer 0 feeding induction heads in layer 1, and neither half works alone. It also carries the lesson that cost me a wrong result: the first version scored every head at 0.9 because a fixed-period task lets a positional reflex masquerade as content matching. The control column is the exercise.
Hung-yi Lee — Machine Learning
NTU · self-attention (上) (下) · slides		 Watch the two self-attention lectures. Mandarin, English slides. Start here. Every figure on this page is from these lectures — so this is the same argument, at full length, from the person who built it. The course is also among the best free ML courses there is, and it keeps running: a 2022 edition and later years carry it into generative models and LLMs.
3Blue1Brown — Attention, step-by-step
Deep Learning ch 6 · ~26 min		 Watch. Nothing to install. Why Q·Kᵀ is a similarity and what the softmax is normalizing. The clearest account of the query/key/value split anywhere.
LLM Visualization
bbycroft.net · browser		 Scrub through a real (tiny) GPT in 3D — every matrix multiply, every head, in sequence. The shapes. Every tensor is drawn at its real dimensions, so n×d stops being notation. Runs a minGPT trained to sort A/B/C, so the whole forward pass fits on screen.
Transformer Puzzles
srush · Colab notebook		 Write programs using only attention and feed-forward ops — reverse a sequence, count tokens, sort. The question this page does not answer: what can attention actually compute? Built on RASP (Thinking Like Transformers). The one to do if you only do one — it is an algorithms exercise, which is your home ground.
Karpathy — Let's build GPT
~2 h, code along → nanoGPT		 Type it out: bigram → self-attention → multi-head → residuals → layer norm. Everything at once, permanently. Ends with the core of nanoGPT, which you then own.

If attention still feels like notation after the first two, do the puzzles rather than re-reading. The gap is usually not "what are Q, K, V" but "what class of computation does this buy" — and that one is only closed by writing something in it.
